clinicalPearls: Defined by a persistent burning or scalding sensation of the oral mucosa, most often the anterior tongue, in the absence of any visible mucosal abnormality
It is a diagnosis of exclusion: the diagnosis of primary (idiopathic) burning mouth syndrome requires that local and systemic causes have been ruled out
Symptoms are frequently accompanied by altered taste (dysgeusia) and a sensation of oral dryness despite normal salivary flow
The burning characteristically builds through the day and may be relieved by eating or drinking, in contrast to organic mucosal disease
It predominantly affects peri- and post-menopausal women and is commonly associated with anxiety, depression, and cancerophobia
Secondary causes to exclude include candidiasis, iron/vitamin B12/folate/zinc deficiency, diabetes, xerostomia, contact allergy, and denture problems
Management combines reassurance, treatment of any contributing factor, and neuropathic agents such as clonazepam (often topical), alpha-lipoic acid, or low-dose tricyclics
reference.pathophysiology: Primary burning mouth syndrome is regarded as a chronic oral neuropathic pain disorder. Evidence points to dysfunction of small-fibre sensory and taste pathways, with degeneration of intra-epithelial nerve fibres, altered central pain processing, and interactions between taste and trigeminal systems; declining gonadal and neuroactive steroid levels around the menopause may contribute. The result is spontaneous burning dysaesthesia without a structural mucosal lesion. Secondary burning mouth symptoms, by contrast, arise from identifiable local or systemic conditions (such as candidiasis, nutritional deficiency, or xerostomia) that irritate or sensitise the oral mucosa.
additionalDifferentials: Nutritional deficiency (iron, vitamin B12, folate, zinc)
Xerostomia (including Sjogren syndrome and drug-induced dry mouth)
Contact stomatitis or allergy to dental materials
additionalInvestigations: Oral examination and swab or smear for Candida
Full blood count with ferritin, vitamin B12, folate, and zinc
Fasting glucose or HbA1c to screen for diabetes
Salivary flow assessment and autoantibody screen if Sjogren syndrome is suspected
Patch testing for suspected contact allergy to dental materials
Assessment of psychological factors including anxiety and depression
redFlags: A visible mucosal ulcer, white patch, or mass, which excludes primary burning mouth syndrome and requires biopsy
Unilateral fixed symptoms with a discrete lesion suggesting malignancy
Rapidly progressive symptoms with systemic illness
Neurological deficits suggesting a central lesion
reference.prognosis: Primary burning mouth syndrome tends to be chronic and fluctuating; a proportion of patients improve spontaneously over time, and many gain partial relief with neuropathic agents and management of psychological factors, though complete resolution is not the norm. Secondary cases resolve when the underlying cause is treated.
pitfalls: Labelling a patient with primary burning mouth syndrome before excluding candidiasis, deficiency states, and xerostomia
Overlooking a subtle mucosal lesion that requires biopsy
Neglecting associated anxiety, depression, or cancerophobia
Assuming reported dry mouth reflects true hyposalivation without measuring salivary flow
Repeatedly investigating without offering symptomatic neuropathic treatment
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
management: Identify and treat secondary causes before diagnosing the primary form, including antifungals for candidiasis, replacement of iron, vitamin B12, folate or zinc deficiency, control of diabetes, and correction of xerostomia, contact allergy or denture problems
Treat primary neuropathic symptoms with topical or systemic clonazepam, a tricyclic antidepressant, a gabapentinoid, or alpha-lipoic acid
Relieve symptoms with saliva substitutes and topical agents such as capsaicin, and advise avoidance of oral irritants
Address psychological factors with reassurance, cognitive behavioural therapy and treatment of anxiety and depression
Educate the patient about the benign but chronic and fluctuating nature of the disorder to counter cancerophobia
Monitor response and refer to oral medicine, neurology, dietetics or psychology within a multidisciplinary approach
